comments.body:
When a child hears their parents fighting, they put their hands over their ears, run into another room, and turn the TV up loud to drown it out. That’s how millions of Americans feel hearing our politics right now—beaten down by a culture stuck in constant shouting mode.

Politicians and pundits know how to get people to listen. Use emotion. Rile them up, frighten them, and they’ll pay attention. But you cannot yell someone into trusting you, and demeaning your opponents only deepens the divisions.

The worst part is that outrage becomes contagious. People begin imitating what goes unchecked, realizing it’s the easiest way to attract attention and followers. Performing righteousness has replaced doing what is right. Elections can’t fix a country where nobody is listening anymore—and most people are just looking for the remote to turn the volume down.

In short, when women enter the public discourse, they are attacked as sexualized, beneath contempt, low-credibility women.  And when their personal experiences might inform the public discourse, they're ignored or silenced.  That women can cleanly separate the personal from the political is a preposterous claim.

KNAPP: “The more complex an electronic system gets, the more accident-prone it is. Sooner or later, it breaks down... A transistor blows, a condenser burns out. Sometimes they just get tired, like people...”

.

When you're a young man.  A man in authority--

--faculties intact!

--you have only to snap your fingers and the minions come running.  And you pass along your instructions. No bother.  No fuss.  

You get older and your minions aren't running to you.  They're walking.  Or ambling. Sauntering.   

And you end up like King Lear. grousing at everyone.  

Mr. Trump is that older man.  At the best of times, he never paid scrupulous attention to what he was saying.  To the words coming out of his mouth.  

But the man is eighty.  And it's as if he were fumbling for the words.  And they're not coming.  But in the meantime--

--there he stands.  At a podium somewhere.  Where he can't just fall silent--

--"Excuse me, ladies and gentlemen.  While I dig up such words as convey what I'm trying to say."  

No no!  He's got to keep talking.  Something he's willing to do in any case.  But now--

--the rabbit's stuck inside the magician's hat.  And has no intention of budging.  And the right words are there somewhere.  But they're not budging.  They refuse to come. 

And so we end up with a U.S. president standing in front of the nation, in front of the world--

--and talking nonsense.  

If he were a better man, I'd feel sorry for him.  

And truth to tell--

--I'm not sure I don't feel sorry for him anyway.  

But not very sorry.  

Thanks, Mr. McWhorter.

I was already aware of options: watchful waiting, radioactive seeds, or a full prostatectomy. Given the biopsy finding, I opted for the prostatectomy. The DaVinci assisted prostate surgery had recently been introduced; my urologist said that he had been trained on the DaVinci machine, but he hadn't had enough experience to recommend it. 

That was 20 years ago. There was loss of sexual function and occasional incontinence. I have lived with that.

BUT, I have acquaintances in their early 50's who weren't made aware of their treatment options after having a small amount of prostate cancer detected. Their surgeons, motivated by profit and not, "Do No Harm", performed DaVinci surgery. One of these men had complications and additional hospital visits. Watchful waiting or radioactive seeds were viable options -- but far less profitable. Loss of sexual function has affected their marriages.

Any man having his PSA measured should be required to be fully informed about treatment options before prostate cancer is actually detected. Surgeons who use panic to have men rush into a surgical procedure are violating their Hippocratic Oath and deserve punishment.

comments.body: Compare the treatment of passengers in the UK and Europe where the government does not see its role as saving airlines money but of ensuring passengers are treated decently. As my flight was delayed for more than five hours, I was entitled to hundreds of dollars in compensation. Luckily, I knew the law. In what could be called premeditated theft United tried to defraud the delayed passengers by fobbing them off with some trivial compensation. I'm sure many of them accepted out of ignorance. When I traveled for business, I did not worry about delays,(other than rescheduling meetings), as I could expense hotels, meals, Ubers, etc. But those experiences now affect how I perceive travel disruptions for personal travel - they are more common than the occasional traveler realizes.

For my trip to Spain this year, I shopped around and found travel insurance for less than the cost of a hotel night - particularly an airport hotel. For an international trip, it also covered medical insurance (sickness or injury) and medical evac.

When not traveling internationally (or frequently), clicking the box for travel insurance when you buy your ticket is looking smarter and smarter. As the article states, airlines frequently manipulate causes to default to something they don't have to pay for. The cost of such a plan is usually much less than the full trip plan we paid for our Spain trip and should cover hotel room and meals if you are stranded.

If you are a frequent, non-business traveler, there are annual plans. For the once or twice a year traveler, the insurance offered by your airline or hotel can offer a little piece of mind.

I was on a flight from Shanghai back to NYC with a layover in Seoul back in 2015. This was on Korean Airline in partnership with Delta. We were delayed several hours in Shanghai due to fog and got into Seoul with 45 minutes to make the connection to NY. Korean Airlines put everyone up at the Grand Hyatt at the airport including a voucher for the excellent buffet and rebooked us on connecting flights in the morning. No paperwork and they even checked our bags onward to the final destination. And since we weren't leaving the airport, did not have to go through customs or anything.

A friend of ours back in the late 80s who was wealthy, middle aged & full of his own importance declined the suggestion when booking a lovely holiday to the "Land of the long, white cloud", for he , his early -twenties son , the son's girlfriend etc.
Turned out to be the biggest mistake of his life & almost the lives of the others.
Deciding to do something completely out of character, he/they went on a beautiful river rapids adventure. The craft capsized, they were all tossed out & our friend was hospitalised for several weeks with incredibly severe leg injuries and more that nearly killed him. The others not so badly hurt.
Just the medical bills in NZ were close to $100kAUD, without needing more back home.
No recourse from the Kiwis either back then (unsure what it's like now) as "every fun" thing was only done by signing a waiver " at your own risk no compensation ". Of course he tried to sue but to no avail.
Travel insurance from then on, was a no-brainer for any of us who knew this man.

comments.body: I'm an old, fat, straight White guy.  I'm a lifelong California resident.  I've been against capital punishment for longer than I can remember.  Pragmatically speaking it's not much of a deterrent.  Morally speaking it's state sanctioned revenge.  If people commit murder they probably need to be removed from contact with others.  There is such a thing as rehabilitation, but we've never worked out a foolproof method to do it.  It's cheaper to execute murderers, but more humane to imprison them.  I go for the humane approach and thank Newsom.

comments.name: GerardM
comments.body:
The author confuses two fundamentally different questions: whether a murderer may morally deserve execution and whether government can be trusted to impose that punishment justly. They are not the same.

Americans have accepted the deliberate taking of human life under circumstances they considered justified, including the firebombing of Tokyo in World War II, which killed roughly 100,000 civilians in a single night. Clearly, the morality of killing has never been regarded as absolute.

The compelling argument against capital punishment is not that executing a murderer is inherently immoral, but that our judicial system is inherently fallible. Wrongful convictions, unequal treatment and irreversible mistakes make the exercise of that power unacceptable. That is a failure of governmental competence, not necessarily of moral principle.

It was nothing like I imagined, as the noise level most of the time was deafening, between inmates yelling & catcalling; continuous, indecipherable announcements being broadcast (comparable to the "sound system" of the NYC subway); and countless music-players of one sort or another competing. All I could think of was Dante's "circles," and a level of chaos that was as close to insanity as I could imagine. The "Adjustment Center," a smaller Death Row Unit that held high security risk inmates & behavioral problem inmates from Death Row (think Richard Ramirez & Scott Peterson), is, medieval. It segregates to prevent interaction, leaving "kites," paper messages passed to the intended recipient by strings & clips that move along the floor from cell to cell. Life without parole in such environments, in my estimation, would be intolerable & traumatic to normal people, and while not death, certainly not a reprieve.

comments.name: Complete

We are watching a torch-carrying mob of modern-day Luddites caught in an existential crisis, in a delusional panic questioning their own necessity. Driven by a fear of the unknown and economic uncertainty, these Americans have manufactured a new 'they'—a phantom entity accused of stealing jobs, siphoning wealth from 'real Americans,' and threatening to replace humanity entirely.

I’ve watched this country shoot itself in the foot for seven decades, but this current moment of uncalled-for, deep-seated insecurity takes the cake. This is by far the biggest cultural shift I have witnessed. The Civil Rights and Women's movements were monumental, though not on this scale. Similarly, the resistance to civil rights wasn't solely fueled by overt bigotry; it was heavily driven by a cultural status quo so deeply ingrained that many couldn't even recognize their own prejudice.

Today’s technological and cultural shift is an order of magnitude greater. It is our first genuine glimpse of the 'flying cars' we were promised in childhood comic books, but it also challenges our ingrained assumptions about human exceptionalism—humanity’s grand and overarching status quo.

Despite the panic, we will adapt. This era will give us a pause for thought, after which we will rebalance our population footprint, heal the planet by destroying it less, and ultimately thrive. The future is bright; it is only this necessary period of adjustment that looks a bit murky.

The American political system may be enormously elastic. Donald Trump is not. Some people never change. They simply become more of who they are. Trump has turned political grievance, personal vengeance and contempt for institutional restraints into defining features of his presidency.

The November 3 electoral repudiation should have been a warning. Instead, Trump continues asserting extraordinary executive authority while treating opposition as an enemy to be crushed rather than citizens to be represented. His vindictive approach to governing has become unmistakable.

Now the spectacle gets uglier. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly points at Howard Lutnick over the failure to restrict Megaspeed despite reported national security concerns. Other officials blame Bessent. Suddenly Trump's celebrated loyalists are scrambling for lifeboats, not accountability.

History offers a warning. Wilson, Truman and Clinton faced Congresses determined to reclaim constitutional authority. Trump now faces that same institutional reckoning.

The difference is a president whose instinct is not compromise but confrontation, whose response to resistance is retaliation.

The tsunami has arrived. Trump's cabinet is pointing fingers, Congress is reclaiming power, and the man who demands absolute loyalty may discover that fear is a remarkably poor substitute for leadership.

From 2003 to 2006, I was a Regional Foreign Service Specialist Officer based in Beijing. As a professional librarian, I spoke to Chinese university students about the internet, research, and fact-checking.

After one lecture in Guangzhou, an attractive young woman, a bit older than the students, asked me to join her for a drink to discuss the talk. I said I was tired and was heading back to my hotel. She pressed, but I declined again.

An hour or two after I got back to my room, the phone rang. It was the same woman, asking to come up and continue the conversation. I said no. When she asked why, I told her — truthfully, since I was married — that my wife wouldn't appreciate it. Back in Beijing, I reported it to the Regional Security Officer, and we laughed at how clumsy the approach was.

What still astounds me is how many Foreign Service Officers in Beijing fell for exactly this setup. They'd have a fling with one of these women, and later an envelope would arrive with photos of the encounter, along with a suggestion that cooperating with Chinese intelligence would keep the photos from their wives or superiors. They'd confess to the Regional Security Officer and get shipped back to Washington — careers over.

Honeytraps are a real tool of Chinese intelligence. I experienced an attempt firsthand, and it still amazes me how many men fell for an approach so unsubtle it was almost comical..

I don't know the exact date, but sometime in the early 1960s, after midnight, 2 friends and I were sitting in the Santa Maria Restaurant at Nassau Avenue and McGuinness Boulevard, when there was the loudest crash sound I have ever heard. We all thought two trucks had collided on the Boulevard, but when we rushed out, we found that a Nassau Avenue house had simply collapsed. It was directly next to a house that had been pulled down to widen McGuinness Blvd.
It looked very much like pictures seen here. Many people rushed over, but were afraid that there might be electrical wiring as such still 'live'. But within 2 minutes, fire engines were there and within 10 minutes huge lights were strung up and rescue operations started. Within 45 minutes, there were neighborhood women who had set up tables along the other side of Nassau Avenue and were serving coffee and whatever to the rescuers (numbering dozens, if not hundreds by then). This happened when mostly everyone was asleep, it was very cold out, but as best I can recall, nobody died as a result. I very slightly knew a girl in that building named Bernadette, and she was apparently okay. It has stayed with me for maybe 65 years, yet it was not nearly as bad as this tragedy looks to be. City inspectors did not do a fully proper job then (and certainly not now), but McGuinness Blvd. was one of Mr. Moses's pet projects, so they probably didn't work too hard in finding fault. So, the more things change, the more they remain the same!

One weekend morning, she said she'd love some lox and cream cheese to go with her sesame. So, we headed across town to Zabars and queued up to the fish counter, which was half a dozen shoppers deep. After hearing how the guy behind the display was rudely dispatching those in front of me--pretty sure it was Saul--I was kinda nervous. When my turn came, he barked, "Yeah? What d'ya want?" I never liked lox and consequently, had never before purchased some. I cleared my throat and whined, "How much is the lox?" Saul barked back, "Six and a quarter." "Oh," I said, relieved, "Six and a quarter a pound." "No," he barked, "Six and a quarter a quarter of a pound!" I felt like an idiot. "Oh, so how many people will a quarter of pound feed," I asked. "Three," he barked, "One will eat and two will watch."

comments.name: Mary TC
comments.body: I visited the Shaker community in Sabbath Day Lake in the summer of 1993.  Besides the beauty of the setting, two things stuck in my mind: that the Shakers invented and patented the old-fashioned clothing pin, which provided the communities with income for many years, and the examples of upholstered Victorian-style furniture that they made and sold—not at all the spare, elegant style we associate with the Shakers. The early Shakers were very pragmatic and practical. Although they lived at a remove from mainstream society, they recognized economic opportunities and supported themselves by participating to some degree in the mainstream economy. That pragmatism may in part explain their longevity. Other, failed Utopian communities should have taken note.

The idea that every act was worshipful produced these simple yet stunning objects that were just so beautiful. It was as if perfection were sought in every act and yet also came from a place of deep humility. In an era where our President just can't find enough gold to gild things with I can still see the warmth of a drawer rendered in butternut and cherry and joined by precisely cut dovetails. We'll never sell our home, because the increase in prices in the last five years means that we can't afford to buy or rent a slightly bigger house (with just one more bedroom) in our neighborhood, and also because who would willingly give up a 2.6% rate to take out a 7% mortgage??? Doing the math on what the payments would be on our home at 7% at what would sell for today, our own home becomes unaffordable for us.  

Of course, that means that we are contributing to the problem of lack of inventory, and lack of sales.  I don't see a way out of this issue until mortgage rates come down, or mortgages become portable.  With portability, I would absolutely be willing to buy the bigger house and sell my current home.    Until then, I guess we are stuck in the small house forever.

We are contributing to the economy by renovating the entire house from top to bottom and inside and out.  We've done major work on every part of our house since we've bought it - new roof, air conditioning, plumbing, electrical, windows four new bathrooms, new floors, closets, kitchen, pool, landscaping,  and everything else you could think of.  We are keeping the contractors and the laborers working, and committing to leaving this house feet first and in a pine box in 30 years.

Over and over again we hear of Ebola continuing to expand in the DRCongo.  The organization MSF (Doctors Without Borders) summed it up well yesterday: “Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many front-line responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets,” says Dr Javid Abdelmoneim, MSF International President. “Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable.”

Indeed it is unacceptable.  But do we not care? 

We live in a world overwhelmed by conflict and rivalries.  Perhaps we have become accustomed to suffering.  Perhaps repeated emergencies have exhausted us.  Perhaps the distance between those dying and those controlling the world's resources makes indifference easier.

Perhaps we just don't care about people dying from Ebola.

The problem with Hollywood is that in its origin stages it was a fairly egalitarian art form.  Then a certain demographic took control under the studio system as a means of syphoning the money to be made (early film had lots of women directors, etc).

This was replaced by the independent film movement of the seventies, but those in control looked much the same.  And today, we have a business with so much nepotism that almost no one not already connected to the existing system can break in. 

Traditional Hollywood is dying because it has become bloated and inbred. I, for one, hope to see this industry break apart. I believe this is the only way it survives the internet threat.

BTW-I have been consumed by film and television since I was a young child in the 60s, the loss of this art form would be personally devastating.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
Hollywood has always looked over its shoulder in fear of government regulation and viewer objection.  For television and radio, sponsors had influence.  Unhappy consumers would write sponsors and that wasn't good.

Very early on Hollywood created a strict moral code, the Hays Production Code, in the hopes of heading off government involvement.  But Hollywood was still criticized over content, such as too many gangster films.  In the 1950s, Hollywood came under the glare of the McCarthyist world and studio heads were pressured to fire suspected communists. Hard times.

In the 1960s, Hollywood faced a changing society, not as morally strict as the past.  But Hollywood had to be careful, because while young people welcomed more contemporary films, older people did not.

Economically, the industry has always been in transition.  Sound movies, radio, television, color, topical themes, cable TV, and now streaming all upended the mix.  Years ago the coming of television killed off the small neighborhood theatre and "B movies" as people stayed home to watch free TV (though some B movie stars did well on TV).

Fast forward to now, Hollywood pushed too hard with DEI and Woke.  It alienated some of its audiences who got tired of the heavy-handed messaging.  But it is not like every person of color has been eliminated from the screen.

One sad aspect is the way corporate America has invaded Hollywood.  We were better off without that invasion.

comments.name: Tom

In her recent essay, Sharon Waxman argues that Hollywood's retreat from diversity initiatives is driven by political pressures and regulatory fears. She misses the most fundamental law of business: supply and demand.
Hollywood did not start falling apart because of Washington politics; it began losing audiences when studios prioritized ideological messaging over pure entertainment. No government regulation forces audiences to skip the theater. Consumers simply vote with their wallets when the product stops delivering escapism, compelling drama, and fun.
If Hollywood wants to rebound, the blueprint isn't found in political maneuvering. It lies in returning to the basics: great stories, great actors, and great movies.
Waxman should study the masters who built the industry by giving audiences what they wanted. Look at great directors like Steven Spielberg, Alfred Hitchcock, Stanley Kubrick, Martin Scorsese, and Kathryn Bigelow. They didn't succeed by checking corporate boxes or catering to political trends. They succeeded through relentless craft, unforgettable characters, and universal storytelling.
When Hollywood focuses on making cinema people want to watch, the box office takes care of itself.

I recently finished reading Sylvester Stallone’s new book, The Steps: A Memoir, so I was especially eager to see I Play Rocky.

I went to the film yesterday in a large Dolby Sound Theatre packed with teenagers and young adults. I’m 65, which made the experience all the more interesting.

While the film stays faithful to the memoir, it leaves out some important details, including his mother’s emotional abuse. She even told him that he was the reason she never had a career because she had him. Undoubtedly and sadly, those experiences played a significant role in shaping the drive and determination that ultimately helped make Stallone successful.

Still, the movie succeeds beautifully on its own merits. It’s thoroughly entertaining, and the young actor portraying Stallone is terrific. He embodies him like no one else.

One of the most enjoyable parts of the experience was watching the audience. They were completely absorbed, laughing at all the right moments, crying at the emotional ones, and even applauding at just the right times.

It’s an uplifting, feel-good movie that clearly resonates across generations. I highly recommend seeing it!

comments.name: ALEX
comments.body:
The article portrays Jensen Huang as a visionary and diplomatic bridge-builder. But above all, he was a ruthlessly profit-driven businessman.

His promotion of “sovereign AI” was a brilliant but cynical sales strategy: convincing governments that technological independence required billions in Nvidia chips, effectively replacing one dependency with another.

His close ties to Donald Trump, access to the White House, and lobbying against US chip export restrictions on China reveal how closely corporate profits and political influence were intertwined.

And one can reasonably wonder how pleased Nvidia's leadership was with the prospect of billion-dollar business through companies like Megaspeed. What Huang personally knew remains an open question, particularly in light of the espionage allegations.

Meanwhile, he relentlessly promoted AI's benefits while downplaying its dangers: mass surveillance, job losses, concentration of power, and serious societal risks.

Huang brilliantly exploited geopolitical tensions, political connections, and governments' fear of falling behind to create enormous business opportunities.

His legacy should not be romanticized. He didn't just fuel the AI revolution. He ruthlessly monetized it, raising serious questions about whether profit repeatedly took precedence over security, ethics, and public accountability.

Mule deer often babysit young in big groups. They will have one  momma deer watch a gang of babies, typically also grouped with yearlings, while the other moms go off to eat and sleep. Then the moms come back to collect their kids and they hang in a loose herd of momma’s, adult daughters/non-mature sons (1-2 years old), and this years babies.

I have a herd that practically lives at my house in the CA mountains and this behavior is very common, I watch it go on all year long. We know individual deer by sight based on physical attributes, behavior and relationships. It’s a complex social structure that would also be beat if a scientist would study it.

On a side note, we also have elk (yes, we have those in Southern CA in a few places) and the deer and the elk will hang in the same locations, but always no closer than 50-100 feet of each other.

comments.name: Agate
comments.body:
Iran's coercion of its citizens and diaspora is vastly underreported, and I appreciate the NYTimes devoting resources to this ongoing story.

The following passage, however, demonstrates that the article is missing important context:  "The seizures have been uniquely effective in extending the government's repressive apparatus far beyond its borders." 

"Uniquely" invites a comparison, but the piece offers none, and "repressive apparatus" is doing a lot of work.

Two pieces of context seem conspicuously absent.

First, financial coercion of the diaspora isn't “new.” In 2017, Iran froze the property rights of 152 current and former BBC Persian staff and contributors. We have examples of precedent, what’s new is the speed and reach.

Second, the regime’s broader “repressive apparatus” includes escalation of both intimidation and violence in Western cities. Pouria Zeraati, who is on the Iran International list you cite, was stabbed in London in 2024. His newsroom had fled London in 2023 following serious threats, returning only six months before the stabbing.

I recognize the article's scope is the expansion of rapid asset seizures, but “unique effectiveness” should not be divorced from Iran’s history of violence. Otherwise, readers cannot fully understand the threat environment and why people on these lists are falling silent.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body: Pretension and posing often rule the day. Now that we are practically speaking in a 1970's redo, I anxiously await someone somewhere to bring back dress clothing with a semblance of quality and real fashion sense that people can wear without being a parody of fashion designer's imaginations. The funny thing is that so many of these people simply recycle cliches of former design eras without adding anything viable. I always look to the Italians to see the matching of quality and comfort with everyday style. That sense of having a harmonious wardrobe that doesn't scream trendy, but influences with grace. The distribution chain of clothiers has been disrupted by fast fashion and disposable clothing. It sounds counter-intuitive but we need to see a re-education of retail executives who are glorified bean counters that have ceased to understand the once magnetic appeal of department stores. There are few of them that know how to train sales people and equip them with the resources to understand not just clothing, but teaching the public how to see quality. As the new generations race to the bottom of online sales, bereft of any experience in real shopping, the influencers cater to an ever shrinking group of groupies. Americans in the main dress deplorably because they've been priced out of quality clothing, and aesthetics in dress is based on the lowest common denominator. The elevation of the T-shirt and jeans has reached its final stage of ubiquity.

comments.body: When I was in grad school and had to give the first presentation for a class in ethics, I was nervous. So nervous, I was visibly shaking; whole body shaking. This was before power point or other similar technology so I was holding my notes in hand, which looked like leaves quaking in the wind. Why pretend I wasn’t nervous? It was obvious. So I quipped, “I’ll be okay once I stop shaking.” I laughed and so did the entire class. Afterwards I received a handful of emails congratulating me on the presentation, saying that I had set a high bar. Now I wonder if that high bar was a result of acknowledging the “uncool,” yet very  human and vulnerable, reality of being nervous.

comments.name: Manahil
comments.body: I believe police officers should be in schools because students deserve to feel safe. Safety matters. Having officers at school can help students feel more protected and make it easier to respond when an emergency happens. They can also help prevent problems and make sure students have someone to turn to when they need help. Schools should be places where students can focus on learning without constantly worrying about their safety, and having trained officers nearby can help create that feeling of security. However I also feel as, officers should treat students with respect and understand that their main job is to protect, not scare or punish them. I think having police officers in schools is important because every student deserves a safe place to learn.

comments.name: David Sells
comments.body: For me personally having a police officer in school at all times ake me feel much safer. They act as a deterant for anyone who may want to harm the students in a school, and I think that is where their influence should end. They should not disciplince students. That should be soley up to school administrators. Having a police officer mixed into the situation for minor issue just cause anxiety and possibly even resentment towards police. Kids shouldn’t distrust police. Which may come from their involvment in any disaplinary scenarios. They should only be there incase of emergency and if any student may be having any serious issues such as abuse at home they could help someone in that sort of situation aswell.

comments.name: Anis B.
comments.body: Law enforcement should be a mandatory addition to all schools worldwide. If there were to be an armed intruder, a school fight, etc, most harm could be prevented by an enforcer. Without them, schools might become places of danger to children, and some students might fear showing up due to safety concerns. This could also cause parents to be worried about their kids, especially as to whether or not they are safe in an educational environment. Safety should be a guarantee. All in all, law enforcement should be implemented in schools across the globe for the sake of the future generation of children.

comments.name: Lily Berthelot
comments.body: I believe police officers make schools safer. Their presence helps students feel protected. Also police officers provide security. Students want a safe environment. Police can prevent dangerous situations. However, teachers should handle minor misbehavior. Officers quickly respond during emergencies. Having them at school gives parents peace of mind.

comments.name: Alexis Crain
comments.body: Schools need to have police officers on campus as it is what keeps us protected. They are necessary. Their role is far more important than just drugs on campus. Some are anxious from police. Although, the police care necessary for life threatening scenarios on campus. It enforces students to be cautious and the police can watch before something bad happens. Police dogs and metal detectors save lives. The police dogs can sniff out dangerous substances and metal detectors stop weapons from being brought into schools. Although kids may feel invaded because of the police, it is necessary to reconsider the big picture of why they are at schools.

comments.name: Alex Koehler
comments.body: I think it is absolutely necessary for cops to be in schools. I don’t fully understand why people would feel intimidated by cops, in school, because they are really just there to keep us safe. Our schools SRO is one of the coolest people in the building, and just his presence makes me feel safer here. I feel if there is no cop instantly present, it opens a window for a lockdown to occur, which then could lead to a much, much worse consequence rather than if there were no cop. Even the cop car sitting outside the school could deter people with bad intentions. I think they having at least one officer per school keeps the children’s safety high, with the addition of security guards too. Cop’s are absolutely necessary.

comments.name: Adelyn F
comments.body: I think everyone has at least one superstition, even if they do not fully believe in them. One superstition I know is that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck. Another common superstition is knocking on wood to avoid bad luck. Personally, I do not believe superstitions can control what happens in my life, but I still sometimes follow them just in case. I think people follow superstitions because they make them feel more comfortable and give them a sense of control. Other common superstitions include walking under a ladder, opening an umbrella inside, and having a black cat cross your path. Even though there is no proof these things cause bad luck, many people still avoid them. I also think superstitions are interesting because they are passed down through families and generations. Parents might teach their children superstitions they learned from their own parents. Over time, these beliefs become traditions. I think superstitions can also be fun because they give people something to talk about. Even if someone does not believe in them, they might still knock on wood just to be safe. Overall, I think superstitions are more about personal beliefs and traditions than facts. I may not believe they can change my luck, but I still think they are interesting and fun to follow.

comments.name: Skye Chiu
comments.body: I had no idea that today was Friday the 13th before I read this article. So, I'm pretty sure that means I lived today like every other day. Today, I did do something different and went to the gym, but I don't think that counts. I'm not that superstitious. For example, I don't believe 7 is a lucky number, or 13 is particularly bad. However, I do believe that your Zodiac influences who you are. Not in the most powerful way, and I know that the month you're born in has nothing to do with your personality, but I just feel that it impacts you in some way. I think superstitions are just a waste of your fear and anxiety. A superstition that I do follow is that before every sports game or swim meet, I don't jinx it. I can't talk about the game before or during, and I really don't like it when teammates congratulate me too much. I stick with it because whenever I do it, I do pretty well. However, I think just writing this is jinxing it. I think people might participate in rituals or beliefs that don't necessarily make sense because it gives them a sense of control. And people really like to be in control, so that's probably why people follow these superstitions.

comments.name: Jada
comments.body: Ironically, today is Friday the 13th, yet I was unaware of that until 3 minutes ago. It’s safe to say I‘m not superstitious about dates like today, but I do know today's supposed to be bad luck because of “the 1916 silent film 'Friday the 13th,' which was adapted from a 1907 novel by Thomas William Lawson.” My mom would be the one to always point out when it was Friday the 13th, but that’s because she is a horror movie enthusiast; I’m definitely not, but I would say I let superstitions control my life from time to time. For example, I don’t put my shoes on the table, not only because that’s gross, but because it’s apparently bad luck, and I’m not going to test it. Towards the bottom of the article, it reads, “really our way of pretending we can control or predict a universe that is uncontrollable and unpredictable”. Last year, I was overly superstitious when it came to preparing for a track meet; the night before my race, I would wear my favorite pajamas with blue monkeys and a hint of yellow, I would then wake up, eat a waffle with chocolate chips, then an energy waffle, and drink out of my green Yeti- with my Electro Light straw. Then when I got to the meet, I would ensure that I did the stretches for equal amounts of time. If  I didn’t do exactly these things, I was entirely convinced that I would run poorly, so I guess this was my way of pretending to control the uncontrollable, but it brought me comfort in times of nervousness.

comments.name: Dylan Kohut
comments.body: For me, Friday the 13th is not anything that I'm genuinely afraid of. When I look at the date and see Friday the 13th, I'm more just thinking of it as a joke rather than anything serious. I'm not a very superstitious person, I have lucky numbers but thats about it for me. I've noticed that many people have numbers that they either like or dislike for whatever reasons. In the article, the author writes, "Part of the issue with 13 is that it follows 12." This is telling us that people have their own reasons for believing why 13 is unlucky. I have a necklace with a shell on it that I found on the beach and I tell myself that it is good luck when I wear it. It has become kind of just a habit to wear it by now. I think that people do rituals or have beliefs that don't make sense because it could be a way of making them feel like they have some control over the future. In the article, the author writes, "All those just become ways for us to try to make sense of the reality that is." This tells us that the reality we live in is unpredictable and we can do things to have it make sense.

comments.body: This article prompts the question, “Does Friday the 13th strike you with fear and worry? Or is it just a normal day?” This really gets me thinking about what I do and don’t believe in which is interesting because I've always just seen it as a “scary day” because of the films but I've never actually been worried about something happening on the actual day. I’m not part of any of the religions that see 13 as a lucky or unlucky number, so I do treat it as a normal day, although over the years, it has gained popularity for being notoriously unlucky, which somewhat affects how I've come to view it. But I do think this is the deal with many things that others view as good or bad which I guess says that I’m not superstitious although I am conditioned to view Friday the 13th as a scary day even though I don’t fully believe it’s unlucky. This is similar to how I view 11:11, ever since I was young, I would always make a wish when it happens to be 11:11 although it’s never come true and I doubt it will. The way I envision these ideas about superstitions is well represented by Sopan Deb’s claim that superstitions are “our way of pretending we can control or predict a universe that is uncontrollable and unpredictable” even though I think they’re very interesting, we aren’t able to accurately predict what is going to happen in the future.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
From the article: "fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization."

We have deniers and delayers leading us over a climate cliff. It’s been 36 years since the first report by the IPCC. 36 years during which we could not plead ignorance yet global emissions of CO2 have increased 70 percent since then.

And the uncertainties seem to be cutting against us as observations show some critical climate systems undergoing changes sooner than expected.

The US has had a number of wakeup calls: floods, wildfires, droughts, heat waves and stronger storms like Hurricane Katrina and New Orleans, Hurricane Sandy and NYC, Hurricane Harvey and Houston and Hurricane Maria and Puerto Rico and Hurricane Florence and the Carolinas.

Although it appears the US slept through the calls, the front desk will keep trying with louder calls for a very long time. It may take something like the erasure of a major city by a strong hurricane to wake us up. Who knows?

Regarding the necessary response to climate change required now due to decades of procrastination, I'm reminded of Alex Honnold's free solo climb of El Capitan, without ropes, and how the climb was like being in the Olympics where if you don't score a "10" you die.

We're in that situation now, if we don't score a 10 on our response to both mitigate coming changes and adapt to what is in the pipeline.

comments.body:
Women who travel? NOTHING beats the unfortunately named 
The Blessings of a Good Thick Skirt: Women Travelers and Their World 
by Mary Russell. From Ancient Roman days to Victorian Days* to present day (up to 1986 when published) it will give you chills, open your eyes and make you wonder "how have it not heard of her? Or her? Or those two??" 

I've never met anyone who's read it. When I recommend it, I get thank you notes in the mail from people! Read it. 

I met Mary while on a Sneem Walking Weekend trail. She was slow, I held back to join her, and it's one of the 10 best decisions I've ever made in my life (and I've had a fabulous life!). 

Don't miss her cycle journey books, too.  Or her story of sailing across the Atlantic. She's a wonder.

*title cones from a diary entry of a typically dressed Victorian woman walking through jungles in Africa trying to locate her not-returned-from-HIS-adventure husband.
